To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mAb806 and 175 bind a misfolded form of EGFR that is found on tumor cells and not normal cells.
the mechanism of mAb806 binding to EGFR is that the peptide epitope is exposed by the local disruption of disulfide bonds.
the mAb806 and the related mAb175 bind to a cryptic epitopes in the EGFR that is exposed only in the context of the EGFR mutant or overexpressed EGFR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing antibodies to EGFR and other proteins that are misfolded or mutated in cancer.
the development of a novel class of antibody-based cancer therapeutics that target the misfolded, activated forms of EGFR.
the development of novel therapeutic agents for the treatment of human tumors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these two antibodies bind to a locally misfoldedd region in EGFR, which is normally inaccessible, but becomes exposed in the mutant form.
the mAb806 and its related antibody mAb175 bind to a cryptic epitopic region on EGFR, which becomes accessible when the EGFR is misfolded, either by mutation, overexpression or autocrine stimulation.
the binding of mab806 and mab175 to wtEGFR requires that the epitope be exposed during receptor activation, or mutation or over expression, and that the epitope is normally inaccessible to antibody.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a novel mechanism of antibody recognition of a wild-type receptor that is activated, mutated, or overexpressed on the surface of tumor cells.
we have developed a new class of antibodies that target a misfolded region on a tumor associated protein.
mAbs mAb175 and mAb806 recognize a cryptic peptide epitope in a misfolded form of wtEGFR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mAb806 antibody can be used to treat tumors that express mutant or overexpressed EGFR.
we have discovered a novel mechanism of antibody recognition, where the binding site is normally occluded, but can be exposed by local misfolding.
we have identified a cryptic epitopes on a wild-type EGFR and have developed an antibody that targets this epitope.
